screens.title: Introduction to Unreal Motion Graphics (UMG)
screens.subtitle: Build interface widgets, show HUD elements, and connect Blueprint UI to C++

narration.text: In this lesson you'll meet Unreal Motion Graphics, or UMG, which is the visual system you use to build in-game user interfaces inside Unreal Engine 5. UMG lets you author Widget Blueprints — assets that describe screens, HUDs, menus, and HUD elements — then instantiate and control them from C++ or other Blueprints. You'll learn the editor panels you use daily: the Palette, Hierarchy, Designer, Details, and Graph, and how those panels map to the widgets you drag and the properties you set. We'll build a compact Player HUD that displays player health and a Menu button, then show how to expose that Widget Blueprint to your Player Controller and add it to the viewport at BeginPlay. Along the way you'll learn panel widgets like Canvas Panel, Horizontal Box, and Vertical Box, when to prefer adaptive layout over absolute placement, and how widget lifecycle events affect performance. By the end you'll have a practical lab-ready workflow: author a WBP_PlayerHUD, wire it to a PlayerHUDClass property, and instantiate it with CreateWidget and AddToViewport so your UI appears in game.

keyIdea.title: What UMG gives you
keyIdea.text: A visual, Blueprint-friendly system for authoring UI assets that are instantiated and controlled from C++ or Blueprints.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will understand the purpose and core components of Unreal Motion Graphics and be able to create a basic Widget Blueprint. You will know how to place common panel widgets such as Canvas Panel, Horizontal Box, and Vertical Box to compose responsive layouts instead of relying solely on absolute coordinates. You will create a WBP_PlayerHUD and add basic UI elements like Text Blocks, Images, and Buttons, and you will learn how to expose that Widget Blueprint to your Player Controller as a TSubclassOf and instantiate it in C++ using CreateWidget, then call AddToViewport to show it on screen. Finally you will recognize the widget lifecycle — Construct, Tick, Destruct — and why placing expensive work in Tick can harm performance. Each objective focuses on practical steps you can perform in the editor and in C++ so you can iterate quickly and keep UI logic organized and maintainable.

screens.title: What is UMG?
screens.subtitle: Unreal's visual UI system and why it exists

narration.text: UMG stands for Unreal Motion Graphics and it is the engine's primary system for authoring in-game user interfaces visually. Rather than writing rendering code for labels and buttons, designers create Widget Blueprints in the UMG editor that compose prebuilt widgets — such as Text Blocks, Images, Buttons, and Progress Bars — into a hierarchical structure. Each Widget Blueprint usually inherits from the C++ base UUserWidget, so the visual asset maps cleanly to C++ classes at runtime. A concrete example is a Player HUD that shows health: you design the layout and styling inside the Widget Blueprint, then a Player Controller creates the widget instance and adds it to the viewport. A common misconception is that UMG is only for designers; in fact UMG integrates tightly with C++ and Blueprint logic, so programmers can instantiate, bind data, and respond to UI events. Key takeaway: UMG separates presentation from game logic, speeding iteration and enabling teams to work in parallel. Ask yourself: which parts of your UI should be visual assets and which should be controlled by gameplay code? What is UMG? means a visual system of widget blueprints built on uuserwidget used to author interactive ui assets.. In practical terms, unreal's visual ui system and why it exists. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Widget Blueprint Anatomy
screens.subtitle: Designer panels: Palette, Hierarchy, Designer, Details, Graph

narration.text: A Widget Blueprint gives you two main spaces: design and logic. In the Designer tab you visually place widgets on a canvas; the Palette holds draggable widgets such as Text Block, Image, Button, and Progress Bar; the Hierarchy panel shows the nested structure of widgets — think of it as a tree of elements. The Details panel lets you inspect and change the selected widget's properties like Text, Font Size, Color, and Anchors. The Graph allows you to add Blueprint logic for interactions and data binding. A concrete workflow: drag a Canvas Panel from the Palette, drop a Text Block onto it, then change the Text property to "Health: 100" in Details, and finally open Graph to bind that Text Block to a variable or event. A frequent misconception is that the Designer is only for static visuals; in reality the Graph and bindings make widgets dynamic. Practice: create a small widget, inspect its Hierarchy, and change a property in Details to see how visuals update immediately. Widget Blueprint Anatomy means palette for widgets, designer for layout, hierarchy for structure, details for properties, graph for logic.. screens.title: Create a Simple Player HUD
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: WBP_PlayerHUD with Canvas, Text Block, and Button

narration.text: Let's walk a concrete creation workflow you can complete in minutes. Step one: in the Content Browser right-click, choose User Interface, then Widget Blueprint and name the new asset WBP_PlayerHUD. Step two: open WBP_PlayerHUD and in the Designer drag a Canvas Panel as the root. The Canvas Panel gives you flexible anchors and offsets for HUD elements. Step three: drag a Text Block onto the Canvas Panel, select it, and in Details set the Text property to "Health: 100" and anchor it to the top-left. Step four: drag a Button onto the Canvas Panel and anchor it to the top-right. Drop a Text Block into the Button and set its text to "Menu". Step five: save the widget. A common error is placing every element with absolute coordinates on Canvas; instead, use anchors so elements stay positioned across resolutions. This short process gives you a functioning HUD asset ready to instantiate from C++ or a controller Blueprint. Try it now to make the steps concrete. screens.title: Panel Widgets: When to use Canvas vs Boxes
screens.subtitle: Canvas Panel, Horizontal Box, Vertical Box, Grid, Overlay, Size Box

narration.text: Panel widgets are the primary building blocks for structuring UI. Canvas Panel provides absolute-style placement with anchors and is excellent for fixed HUD elements, but using Canvas for entire layouts often breaks responsiveness. Horizontal Box and Vertical Box arrange children automatically in a row or column; use them for inventories, menus, and grouped controls where order matters. Grid Panel places children into cells and is handy for uniform icon grids. Overlay stacks widgets; use overlay to place a pop-up atop a dimmed background. Size Box enforces dimensions on its child, useful when you need a consistent control size. A concrete contrast: place your health text and small buttons in a Canvas anchored to corners, but build a main menu with a Vertical Box so buttons stack and scale cleanly. A common mistake is positioning menu items with pixels in Canvas — instead, use Boxes and Grid for maintainable layouts. Key takeaway: mix Canvas for HUD anchors and boxes/grids for adaptive content. Panel Widgets: When to use Canvas vs Boxes means use canvas for anchored hud pieces; use horizontal/vertical/ grid for adaptive, maintainable layouts.. In practical terms, canvas panel, horizontal box, vertical box, grid, overlay, size box. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Horizontal Box
Arranges children in a horizontal row; ideal for condensed counters like ammo and health bars.
Vertical Box

Key Takeaway

Choose panels that express the relationship you want: flow (boxes), grid (grid), stacked overlays (overlay), anchored HUDs (canvas).

screens.title: Expose the Widget to C++ and Instantiate It
screens.subtitle: TSubclassOf, UUserWidget*, CreateWidget, and AddToViewport

narration.text: To show your WBP_PlayerHUD at runtime, you expose its class to the Player Controller as a TSubclassOf property and then create an instance with CreateWidget. In C++, declare a property such as TSubclassOf PlayerHUDClass and a UUserWidget* PlayerHUD instance pointer. In BeginPlay call a helper that checks PlayerHUDClass, calls CreateWidget with this controller as the owner and PlayerHUDClass as the class, and then calls AddToViewport on the returned instance. A concrete safety check is to verify PlayerHUDClass is set, because CreateWidget requires a valid class. A common misconception is that assigning the Blueprint asset path in C++ is the only way; instead, expose the TSubclassOf and set the asset in a Blueprint subclass of your controller for flexibility. Key takeaway: keep the class reference as editable in Blueprints and instantiate in BeginPlay, so designers can swap UI without recompiling C++. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Expose & Instantiate
Starter C++ pattern
// Header (relevant parts)
UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "UI")
TSubclassOf<UUserWidget> PlayerHUDClass;

UPROPERTY()
UUserWidget* PlayerHUD;

// Source (relevant parts)
void AMyPlayerController::BeginPlay()
{
  Super::BeginPlay();
  CreateAndAddPlayerHUD();
}

void AMyPlayerController::CreateAndAddPlayerHUD()
{
  if (PlayerHUDClass)
  {
    PlayerHUD = CreateWidget<UUserWidget>(this, PlayerHUDClass);
    if (PlayerHUD)
    {
      PlayerHUD->AddToViewport();
      UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Player HUD created and added to viewport."));
    }
  }
  else
  {
    UE_LOG(LogTemp, Error, TEXT("PlayerHUDClass is not set in MyPlayerController!"));
  }
}
Explanation
  • Make the TSubclassOf editable so designers assign the Blueprint asset.
  • CreateWidget returns a UUserWidget instance you store and manage.
  • Call AddToViewport to make the widget visible to the player.
Key Takeaway

Expose the class to Blueprints, create the widget in BeginPlay, and log errors if the class is unset.

screens.title: Blueprint Binding & Game Mode
screens.subtitle: Assigning PlayerHUDClass in BP_MyPlayerController and configuring GameMode

narration.text: Once your PlayerController exposes PlayerHUDClass, the usual workflow is to create a Blueprint subclass of that controller and assign the Widget Blueprint asset in the Details panel. For example, create BP_MyPlayerController derived from your C++ AMyPlayerController, open it, select the PlayerHUDClass variable, and assign WBP_PlayerHUD. Next, edit your Game Mode Blueprint (for example BP_YourGameMode) and set the Player Controller Class to BP_MyPlayerController. When the game starts, the engine will create an instance of your Blueprint controller class which retains the C++ logic to CreateWidget and AddToViewport. A common misconception is that C++ alone must set the widget class; allowing designers to set the class in Blueprint enables rapid iteration and swapping UIs without recompiles. Test this by running Play In Editor and confirming the log message and the visual HUD appear. If the widget doesn't show, verify the Game Mode uses your controller and that PlayerHUDClass has a valid asset assigned. screens.title: Widget Lifecycle and Performance
screens.subtitle: Construct, Tick, Destruct — where to do work

narration.text: UMG widgets have lifecycle events that mirror actor lifecycles. Construct is called when a widget is created and added to the viewport — treat it as initialization time for binding events, preparing animations, and setting default values. Tick runs every frame for widgets that enable ticking; avoid putting expensive calculations in Tick because UI Tick runs every frame and can harm performance. Destruct runs when a widget is removed or destroyed — clean up bindings and timers here. A concrete example: bind a button click to a handler in Construct rather than scanning for button references in Tick. A common misconception is to update UI values by polling in Tick; instead, push updates from gameplay code or use events and data bindings so updates occur only when state changes. Key takeaway: prefer event-driven updates and initialization in Construct to keep UI responsive and efficient. Widget Lifecycle and Performance means initialize in construct, avoid heavy work in tick, and clean bindings in destruct for predictable performance.. In practical terms, construct, tick, destruct — where to do work. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle rule
keyIdea.text: Initialize in Construct, avoid heavy work in Tick, and clean bindings in Destruct for predictable performance.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Widget Lifecycle
Lifecycle events
Construct: widget initialization, bind events, prepare visuals.
Tick: called every frame if enabled — avoid expensive operations here.
Destruct: clean up timers and event bindings when widget is removed.
Concrete example
Bind a button's OnClicked delegate in Construct rather than searching for buttons inside Tick every frame.
Performance tip
If you need per-frame updates, limit the data updated and consider throttling to fewer frames or using event-driven state pushes from gameplay code.
Key Takeaway

Prefer Construct for setup and event-driven updates over Tick to preserve runtime performance.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
screens.subtitle: Absolute positioning, missing AddToViewport, and performance traps

narration.text: Developers often run into a handful of recurring issues when learning UMG. First, over-relying on Canvas Panel absolute coordinates leads to brittle layouts that break on different resolutions — the fix is to use anchors, Horizontal and Vertical Boxes, or Grid Panels for adaptive content. Second, creating a widget instance without calling AddToViewport means the widget exists but is never visible; remember to call AddToViewport or SetVisibility appropriately. Third, placing heavy operations in Tick inside widgets can create frame-time spikes; move initialization to Construct or perform updates only on events. Fourth, forgetting to assign the PlayerHUDClass in BP_MyPlayerController means CreateWidget has no class to instantiate; make the property EditAnywhere and verify the Blueprint assignment. For debugging, add UE_LOG calls after creating the widget and verify the Game Mode is using your controller. By recognizing these mistakes early, you can iterate faster and avoid wasted debugging time. Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them means use anchors and panels for layout, call addtoviewport, avoid tick-heavy work, and confirm class assignments.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Assessment Idea: Toggle an Inventory Screen
screens.subtitle: C++ steps to show and hide UI on a key press

narration.text: A useful assessment is implementing an inventory screen that toggles when the player presses a key. The C++ steps are straightforward. First, declare a TSubclassOf InventoryClass and a UUserWidget* InventoryWidget pointer in your PlayerController. Add a boolean flag bIsInventoryOpen to track visibility. In BeginPlay create the widget instance but do not immediately add it to the viewport, or create it on first use. Bind an input action for the inventory key. In the input handler check whether the widget exists and whether bIsInventoryOpen is true. If the inventory is closed, call AddToViewport and set bIsInventoryOpen true; if it is open, call RemoveFromParent or SetVisibility to collapse it and set bIsInventoryOpen false. A common nuance is deciding whether to keep the widget in memory when hidden; RemoveFromParent frees the visual but you can keep the pointer and re-add for faster re-opening. This task tests lifecycle, class exposure, input binding, and state management in a single practical feature. Key Takeaway

The toggle pattern combines UI instantiation, input binding, and state tracking — a compact test of UMG integration.

screens.title: Design for Iteration and Teamwork
screens.subtitle: Separate visuals from game logic and expose classes to designers

narration.text: A practical design strategy is to separate UI presentation from gameplay logic. Keep the Widget Blueprints focused on visuals, layout, and local behavior such as simple animations or button visuals. Put gameplay-driven updates and state decisions in controllers, game state, or player state, and push changes into the widget through a well-defined interface such as public functions or event dispatchers. Expose the widget class as Editable in the PlayerController so designers can swap assets without C++ changes. A concrete workflow: gameplay code updates a health variable, then calls a public UpdateHealth function on the HUD widget that sets the Text Block accordingly. A common misconception is trying to embed complex game rules inside the UI; this makes the UI brittle and hard to reuse. Key takeaway: define a small A P I on your widgets for updates and let gameplay own the state. This keeps iteration fast and responsibilities clear across team roles. Interface pattern
Let gameplay code own state and call small widget functions to update visuals. Example: PlayerState updates health and calls HUD->UpdateHealth(newHealth) instead of the widget polling the PlayerState.

Team workflow

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Quick reference of the chapter's essential terms

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important concepts you should remember. UMG is Unreal's visual UI system used to author Widget Blueprints that map to the UUserWidget base class. Widget Blueprints are assembled inside the UMG editor using panels such as Canvas Panel, Horizontal Box, Vertical Box, Grid Panel, Overlay, and Size Box. In C++ you expose a TSubclassOf of UUserWidget on a PlayerController, create the widget at runtime with CreateWidget, and show it with AddToViewport. Widget lifecycles include Construct for initialization, Tick for per-frame updates (avoid heavy work here), and Destruct for cleanup. By separating visual presentation from game logic and using panel widgets for adaptive layouts, you make interfaces more maintainable and performant. Keep this list as your mental checklist when building UI: design, expose, create, show, and manage lifecycle — and always favor event-driven updates for efficiency.

keyIdea.title: Summary
keyIdea.text: Design Widget Blueprints, expose classes, create runtime instances, and prefer event-driven updates for performance.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three compact cards to anchor memory

narration.text: Keep three short ideas in mind as you practice. First, Widget Blueprints are the visual assets that define your UI; treat them as presentation and use the Graph only for UI-specific behavior. Second, prefer panel widgets for layout — use Canvas for anchored HUD pieces and boxes or grids for adaptive content so your UI scales across resolutions. Third, integrate UMG with C++ by exposing a TSubclassOf, creating an instance with CreateWidget, and showing it with AddToViewport, while managing lifecycle events for performance. These three concepts — visual asset, layout choice, and instantiation pattern — form a reliable mental model for building and maintaining UIs in Unreal Engine. When in doubt, ask: who owns the state, how does the UI scale, and is this created and torn down at the right time?
